justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, anchored to what I'd expect from a stable, large-cap equity or index instrument trading near the 336–338 range. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 336.5 essentially assumes mean reversion or very slight positive drift from the current price, with no major catalyst expected to shift the price dramatically in either direction. At one week, the estimate nudges up slightly to 338, reflecting the general historical tendency of equity markets to drift upward over short periods in the absence of negative shocks. At one month, 342 continues that gradual drift, consistent with an annualized return assumption in the mid-single digits applied over roughly 20 trading days.

The confidence interval widths grow systematically with the time horizon, which reflects the square-root-of-time scaling typical of random walk models. At one day, a 23-point range (325–348) captures typical intraday-to-overnight volatility plus some tail risk. By one week, the range widens to 47 points (315–362), accounting for the accumulation of daily volatility over five sessions. At one month, the 95-point range (295–390) reflects that over roughly 20 trading days, a broad variety of macro and micro outcomes become plausible. Implied volatility levels, recent realized volatility in the underlying instrument, and general market conditions all fed into calibrating these widths.

The key sources of uncertainty include macroeconomic data releases such as inflation prints, employment reports, and central bank communications, any of which could sharply reprice risk assets. Geopolitical developments or sudden shifts in credit conditions could amplify volatility well beyond normal ranges. At the one-month horizon especially, earnings season dynamics or a policy surprise from a major central bank could easily push the price outside the stated 295–390 interval.

The most acute tail risks that could violate even the 90% intervals would be a financial contagion event, an unexpected geopolitical escalation, or a sudden liquidity crisis that causes correlated selling across asset classes. On the upside, an unexpectedly strong economic data series or a dovish policy pivot could trigger a sharp rally beyond 390. These low-probability but high-impact events are precisely what the tails of the distribution are meant to capture, though by construction they are assigned only a 10% combined probability across both tails.
